content:
I discovered that Appa was much larger when there was nothing between me and the ground but several thousand feet of air.

“You’re doing great!” Aang shouted over the wind.

“I’m gripping fur with muscles I didn’t know existed!”

“That counts!”

We were flying north of Cranefish Town to survey a possible road through the hills. The council wanted a map before winter. Toph had refused to come because, in her words, “flying is just falling while Twinkle Toes lies about it.” Katara had stayed behind at the clinic.

That left Aang and me alone on Appa’s saddle.

It had seemed less significant on the ground.

In the sky, every glance felt larger.

Appa’s back moved beneath us like a slow ship. The world below became patches of green, river silver, and tiny roofs. Aang sat forward with the reins loose in his hands. Wind curled around him as naturally as breath.

He looked at home in a way I had never seen him look inside council chambers.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“Do all of you say that?”

He looked over his shoulder, smiling. “Toph says it because she likes making people nervous.”

“And you?”

“I was hoping you were.”

My stomach dropped harder than it had when Appa climbed.

Aang laughed at my expression, then immediately softened. “Sorry.”

“Don’t apologize.”

“I don’t want to make you uncomfortable.”

“You’re not.”

The words came out honest enough that Toph would have approved.

Aang turned forward again, but I could see the red at the tips of his ears.

We landed on a grassy ridge near midday.

The proposed road would cut through a low valley between two farming villages. From above it looked easy. On the ground I found burial markers half-hidden in tall grass.

Aang found them at the same time.

His entire posture changed.

He knelt beside the nearest stone. The carving was old Earth Kingdom script, weathered but legible.

“This road can’t go here,” he said.

“We can reroute.”

“The engineers said the other route adds twelve miles.”

“Then it adds twelve miles.”

He looked at me.

I shrugged. “People are inconvenient even after they die.”

Aang smiled sadly.

We walked among the stones until we found the edge of the burial ground. I marked it on the map. Aang placed fallen offerings upright and cleared weeds from names he could read.

“You do this a lot,” I said.

“What?”

“Carry people you never met.”

He sat back on his heels.

For a while he said nothing.

The wind moved through the grass.

“When I woke up,” he said, “everyone I knew was gone.”

I had heard the story, of course. Everyone had. Hearing it as history was different from hearing it in Aang’s voice.

“I was twelve,” he continued. “And people kept telling me I had to save the world. They meant well. Most of them.” His fingers traced the edge of the stone. “But sometimes it felt like they were asking me to fix something because I was the last person left who could be blamed for not preventing it.”

I sat beside him.

“You didn’t cause the war.”

“I know that now.”

“Do you?”

His head turned.

I expected defensiveness.

Instead he exhaled.

“Some days.”

There it was again: his willingness to leave a door open where certainty would have been easier.

He looked across the valley. “I want to rebuild the Air Nation.”

The sentence carried more weight than the map between us.

“I know.”

“I don’t mean buildings.”

“Culture.”

“People. Traditions. Stories. Ways of thinking.” He picked a blade of grass and rolled it between his fingers. “I’m one person. Sometimes everyone talks about the future like I’m supposed to create it by myself.”

I understood the shape of that pressure even if I could never understand its size.

“You can teach people.”

“I do.”

“You can preserve records.”

“I do.”

“You can make sure Air Nomad ideas survive without turning yourself into a machine for producing descendants.”

Aang stared at me.

I realized how bluntly I had said it.

“Sorry.”

Then he laughed.

Not because it was funny. Because something had broken open.

“Toph is rubbing off on you.”

“That’s horrifying.”

“She’d be proud.”

Aang lay back in the grass with his hands behind his head.

I hesitated, then lay beside him.

Clouds moved overhead.

“I do want children someday,” he said.

“Okay.”

“With Katara. If she wants them.”

“She probably wants to be asked more than she wants the world to assume.”

“Exactly.”

He turned his head toward me.

“And if my family looks different than people expect…”

The unfinished sentence settled between us.

My pulse began doing unhelpful things.

Aang smiled a little.

“Toph isn’t here,” he said.

“Good.”

“But I can still tell when you’re nervous.”

“I’m not nervous.”

“You’re flattening the map with both hands.”

I released it.

Aang laughed again.

I pushed his shoulder.

He rolled with it dramatically, as if I had knocked the Avatar off a cliff.

“You attacked a peaceful monk.”

“You survived.”

“Barely.”

He caught my wrist when I tried to shove him again.

The playfulness stopped without disappearing.

His hand was warm around mine.

Neither of us moved.

The wind seemed suddenly louder.

Aang’s gaze dropped to our joined hands, then lifted to my face.

“I like you,” he said.

It was absurdly direct.

Of course it was.

“I had noticed.”

“Katara likes you too.”

My breath caught.

“That is a much more dangerous sentence.”

He grinned. “Toph likes you.”

“No, Toph enjoys tormenting me.”

“That’s how Toph likes people.”

I stared at the sky.

“This is complicated.”

Aang released my wrist, though his fingers brushed mine on the way.

“Yeah.”

“You said loving Katara wasn’t complicated.”

“It isn’t. People are.”

“And you’re okay with that?”

He considered the question seriously.

“I think love has to make room for truth.”

“That sounds like something you practiced before saying.”

“It sounded better in my head.”

I laughed.

Aang smiled, pleased.

We finished the survey in the afternoon and marked a longer route around the burial ground.

On the flight home, I sat closer to him than I had on the way out.

Not touching.

Almost.

Cranefish Town appeared on the horizon as the sun lowered, smoke and roofs glowing gold.

Aang looked back at me.

“For the record,” he said, “I’m glad you came.”

“To the survey?”

“To town.”

The wind stole whatever answer I might have given.

Maybe that was mercy.

Maybe it was cowardice.

Either way, when Appa descended, I found my hand resting near Aang’s on the saddle.

Close enough that the space between our fingers felt deliberate.

Air had never seemed so heavy.

After we landed, Aang pretended not to notice that my legs needed several seconds to remember they belonged to the ground.

He was very bad at pretending.

“First flight?” he asked.

“You know it was.”

“I thought maybe you secretly traveled by sky bison all the time.”

“Constantly. I simply never mentioned my extensive bison network.”

Appa huffed beside us, which Aang accepted as support for his argument.

We walked toward the ridge while the others unpacked lunch. Aang kept his pace slower than usual. Not enough to feel like pity. Just enough that I did not have to ask.

“That part up there,” I said, pointing back toward the open sky, “when there was nothing under us—does it ever scare you?”

He looked honestly surprised.

“The flying?”

“The falling.”

Aang’s expression changed. Some of the playfulness remained, but something older moved behind it.

“Sometimes,” he admitted. “Not usually from Appa.”

I understood the rest without him saying it.

He nudged a pebble with his sandal. “People think airbenders don’t get attached because we learn that everything changes. That’s not the same as not caring when something can be lost.”

I watched the pebble roll down the path.

“So what do you do?”

“Pay attention while I have it.”

The answer was almost unbearably Aang: simple enough to sound easy, difficult enough to take a lifetime.

Behind us, Katara called that if we wanted dumplings we had better hurry before Toph found the basket.

“Too late!” Toph yelled.

Aang grabbed my hand without thinking and ran.

I ran with him.

This time, the space between our fingers disappeared.

At lunch, Aang kept glancing at our joined hands as though he had discovered a new kind of bending. I finally squeezed his fingers.

“Stop staring.”

“I’m not staring.”

“You’re terrible at lying.”

From across the blanket, Toph said, “Confirmed.”

Katara laughed.

Aang leaned closer and whispered, “Still okay?”

The question mattered more than the touch.

“Yes.”

His thumb brushed mine once, light as moving air. The mountain wind tugged at our clothes, Appa snored in the grass, and nobody asked the moment to become larger than it was.

When we joined the others, Aang let go only after asking with his eyes. I answered by squeezing once before I did. The choice made the distance feel intimate instead of empty.
